lesson.title: The Symbol Itself: Sigma Notation
lesson.summary: Sigma notation, written with the capital Greek letter Σ, is the actual symbolic shorthand that turns a long sum like 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 into a single compact expression.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter argued that long, patterned sums need a compact way to be written down. Sigma notation is that compact way. It uses the capital Greek letter Σ, sigma, chosen because it is the Greek letter that corresponds to S, for sum, to mean add up the following expression for every value of the index in the given range. A sigma expression has four parts: the sigma symbol itself, a lower limit written below it, where the index starts, an upper limit written above it, where the index stops, and a formula to the right of the sigma, what gets added at each step.

In symbols, Σ (from i=1 to n) of a_i means a_1 + a_2 + a_3 and so on through a_n. Every value of i from the lower limit to the upper limit, inclusive, gets plugged into the formula a_i, and all of the resulting terms are added together. The letter used for the index, commonly i, j, or k, does not carry any special meaning of its own, it is just a placeholder that tracks which term of the sum you are currently generating.

Take the sum of the first four perfect squares from the previous chapter, now written in sigma notation: Σ (from i=1 to 4) of i². Expanding it means plugging in i=1, then i=2, then i=3, then i=4, and adding the results: 1² + 2² + 3² + 4² = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30. The compact form and the expanded form describe exactly the same sum, sigma notation has not changed the value, only how much space it takes to write it down.

Sigma notation is exactly what makes the Riemann sum formula precise. Using the same partition as earlier chapters, f(x) = x² on the interval from 0 to 2 with n = 4 and Δx = 0.5, the right Riemann sum can be written as Σ (from i=1 to 4) of f(x_i) Δx, where x_i is the right endpoint of the i-th subinterval. Expanding it: f(0.5)Δx + f(1.0)Δx + f(1.5)Δx + f(2.0)Δx = (0.25)(0.5) + (1.0)(0.5) + (2.25)(0.5) + (4.0)(0.5) = 0.125 + 0.5 + 1.125 + 2.0 = 3.75, matching the value computed the long way back in the right Riemann sum chapter. In general form, this same idea is written Σ (from i=1 to n) of f(x_i) Δx, and that single line of notation is the standard way an approximating sum for a definite integral is written.

Sigma notation is a direct upgrade of the summation notation idea from the previous chapter: the same underlying concept, a repeated pattern added across a range, now expressed with a specific, universally recognized symbol. The next chapter zooms in on one more detail of this notation: the index of summation itself, what it means for it to be a dummy variable, and how to shift it around without changing the value of the sum.
